items.claim: Where a privileged group is granted PowerShell Remoting access to a host, adding the account to that group is sufficient to obtain a remote session on the server with no credential of its own.
items.body:
Where a privileged group is granted PowerShell Remoting access to a host, adding the account to that group is sufficient to obtain a remote session on the server with no credential of its own.

items.disproof: After joining the group the PowerShell Remoting connection is refused or fails authorization, meaning the group carries no remoting rights on that host.

During the penetration test the penetration tester got access to a machine called examvm and got a user called studentuser after some enumeration the penetration tester found that the student user Generic Write on a group called “CompanyAdministrators” so the penetration tester added himself to the “ComapanyAdministrators” and on checking the access of this group the penetration tester found the the “CompanyAdministrators” group members have Local Administrator access on the examvm machine so the penetration tester was now elevated to administrator after that the penetration tester dumped the memeory to find a username named “sharemanager” and his password in Clear-Text format in memory the penetration tester logged in as the “sharemanager” user and started enumerating the shares to find out that the sharemanager has access to a share named ”ScheduledQueries” on the “SRV71” server on checking the ”ScheduledQueries” share the penetration tester find a file named “Queries.ps1” which was a PowerShell script running every 5 mins on checking the access to this script it appears that the penetration tester can modify the script so he decided to put a malicious Reverse Shell in the file to get a connection back to him and after 5 mins the penetration tester gained access to the “SRV71” server and running as a user named “sqlconnector” after deep enumeration the penetration tester found a MSSQL Instance on the “Glacis.corp” domain on testing the accessibility with the user “sqlconnector” it turns out that we have access to the MSSQL Server the penetration tester then enumerated the users that could be impersonated and found two users which was “sqlsrva3dm” and “sa” the penetration tester impersonated those users and activated the “xp_cmdshell” function and gained remote code execution on the “sqlsrv3” Server as “nt authority\system” the penetration tester then dumped the credentials form the memory to find that there was a user named “dbmaster” and it’s hash on enumeration it turs out the “dbmaster” user has constrained delegation on the “glacis-dc” so the penetration tester abused that and got access to the ldap service on the “galcis-dc” on getting access to the ldap service the penetration tester performed the DCSync attack to retrive the hash of “glavice\Administrator” and then OverPass-The-Hash to gain access as the “Administrator” after that the penetration tester dumped the credentials from “Glacis-dc” and got the user “glacis-dc$” after enumeration the penetration tester found out that the “glacis-dc$” can add members to a group named “pawadmins” so the penetration tester added his “studentuser” to “pawadmins” group on checking the PowerShell Remoting access the penetration tester got access to the “pawsrv” Server and on enumeration he found that the users of “pawadmins’ group have local admin access on “pawsrv” the penetration tester dumped the credentials and got the hash of “pawsrv$” on enumeration it turns out that the “pawsrv$” have DCSync rights on “citadel.corp” the penetration tester performed the DCSync attack and extracted the hash of the user “Citadel\Administrator” then the penetration tester OverPass-The-Hash as the “Administrator” then PowerShell Remote to the “Citadel-dc” finally the penetration tester added the “studentuser” to the “Domain Admins” group to maintain the access in the network

You can also obtain hardware and system data from WS-Management protocol implementations running on operating systems other than Windows in your enterprise. WinRM establishes a session with a remote computer through the SOAP-based WS-Management protocol rather than a connection through DCOM, as WMI does.
WinRM is the name of both a Windows service and a protocol that allows a user to interact with a remote system (e.g., run an executable, modify the Registry, modify services).
